analysis.one_liner: Restricts aggressive medical debt collection and creates a public database of collectors' practices.
analysis.headline: The bill to rein in medical debt collection never got a hearing or vote in the Senate committee it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have restricted how hospitals and their debt collectors go after patients' medical bills. Hospitals would have had to wait 180 days after the first bill before taking severe steps like wage garnishment, liens, or credit reporting; stop collecting while a patient's insurance appeal is pending; first check whether the patient qualifies for charity care or public assistance; and send itemized statements, payment receipts, and language-assistance information. It also would have created a public, searchable database of which debt collectors hospitals use and who gets hit with lawsuits and garnishments, broken down by race, gender, and ZIP code.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with medical bills — especially uninsured and lower-income patients who are most likely to face lawsuits, wage garnishment, liens on their homes, or damage to their credit scores. The bill would have capped what nonprofit hospitals could collect from uninsured patients at the "generally billed" amount, forced collection to pause during insurance appeals, and required screening for financial assistance before any collection began. The public database would also have given journalists, regulators, and researchers a window into which collectors sue whom.

how_it_helps.text: Bars hospitals and their collectors from starting severe collection actions — wage garnishment, bank account attachments, liens, credit reporting, lawsuits, arrest warrants — until 180 days after the first bill is sent, and requires them to halt such actions if a patient notifies them that a health insurance appeal is pending.

Requires hospitals to determine whether a patient qualifies for a federal or state assistance program or the hospital's own charity care — and refer the patient there — before any collection activity starts, and caps what nonprofit hospitals may collect from uninsured patients at the amount generally billed to insured patients.

Gives patients an easy-to-understand itemized statement before collection begins, detailed receipts of payments within 30 days, and information about language-assistance services for people with limited English proficiency, and requires collectors to confirm they have the right person before collecting.

Creates a public, searchable database in which health care entities must annually report which debt collectors they use or sell debt to, what collection practices they pursue, and — broken down by race, ethnicity, gender, and ZIP code — whose debts get referred to collectors and sued over, plus penalties patients can enforce in court, including class actions with damages up to $2 million or 1% of the provider's annual net income.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other health care providers, and the medical debt collection industry they hire or sell debt to. Providers would face new reporting duties, a 180-day waiting period, restrictions on collecting from uninsured patients above the standard billed amount, and lawsuit exposure with attorney's fees if they violate the rules. Nonprofit hospitals that routinely sue uninsured patients for full charges would lose the most.

drawbacks.text: The 180-day waiting period and required assistance screening could slow cash flow for hospitals, and small physician practices and rural critical-access hospitals — which the bill covers unless the Health and Human Services Secretary exempts small practices — could face compliance burdens out of proportion to their collections activity.

Providers facing new class-action exposure with statutory damages and attorney's fees would likely pass some costs on through pricing or expand the use of medical credit cards and payment plans to collect earlier in the process, shifting rather than reducing collection pressure.
The bill leaves the definition of 'health care entity' largely to the Secretary of Health and Human Services, so its real reach would depend heavily on how a future administration wrote the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefits are concrete: a mandatory pause before garnishments and lawsuits, screening for charity care, itemized bills, and a public record of who gets pursued for medical debt. The costs fall on providers and collectors, and the main honest concerns are compliance burden for small practices and the possibility that providers restructure their collection tactics. The bill's reach did depend on regulatory definitions, but its core protections were specific and enforceable by patients in court.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, joined by Republican Sen. Mike Braun, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill remained in committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, medical debt collectors, and credit-reporting interests are better off, because the collection restrictions, the uninsured-charge cap for nonprofit hospitals, and the public database of collection practices were never enacted. Patients facing aggressive medical debt collection gained nothing from this attempt.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restrict medical debt collection and create a public collection database.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — on the bill after it was referred on July 25, 2023, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate majority leadership, which controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with no committee action, it never had a path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat and cosponsored by a Republican, and its opponents were simply inaction: no group ever had to vote against it on the record.

industries.note: Nonprofit hospitals are already required to have charity care policies but are frequently sued over aggressive collection of uninsured patients' bills; this bill would have capped what they can collect from the uninsured and forced them to screen for assistance first, with class-action exposure if they failed. Hospital-owned facilities, nursing homes, and physician group practices were all covered.

Debt collectors working for health care entities would have faced a 180-day waiting period, mandatory debtor-identity checks, and public annual reporting of their lawsuits, garnishments, and liens — including who they target by race and ZIP code. The CFPB report provision was aimed at improving supervision of exactly this industry.

Reporting medical debt to credit bureaus counts as an extraordinary collection action, so the 180-day waiting period and appeal-related holds would have cut the flow of new medical tradelines. The bill also required CFPB reports drawing on anonymized data from the three largest bureaus, pulling them further into federal scrutiny of medical debt.
